lesson.title: LINE Them Up: The Four Conditions for Trusting a Regression Slope
lesson.summary: Before trusting a t-test or t-interval for a regression slope, four conditions, remembered as LINE (Linearity, Independence, Normality of residuals, Equal variance), all need to be reasonably satisfied.
lesson.body:
The last four chapters covered four separate assumptions, one at a time. It's worth collecting them in one place, because every t-test and t-interval for a slope from this whole unit leans on all four simultaneously. The mnemonic LINE keeps them straight: Linearity, does a straight line actually describe the relationship, checked with a residual plot looking for curvature. Independence, are the observations unrelated to each other, justified by how the data were collected rather than by any plot. Normality of residuals, are the leftovers roughly normally shaped, checked with a histogram or normal probability plot of the residuals. Equal variance, does the scatter around the line stay a consistent width across the full range of x, checked by looking for fanning in the residual plot.

One thing worth noticing about that list: three of the four, linearity, normality, and equal variance, are checked using plots of the data itself, mostly variations on the residual plot. Independence stands apart, checked by reasoning about the study's design. A residual plot that looks flawless cannot rescue a dataset with an independence problem, streaky time-series residuals or clustered measurements will not show up as curvature or fanning. And conversely, a well-designed random sample doesn't guarantee linearity or equal variance. All four need their own separate check.

It's also worth being realistic about what 'checking a condition' means in practice. No real dataset satisfies any of these four perfectly. The task, on the AP exam and in real analysis, is never to declare conditions definitively 'met' or 'violated' as if they were a yes or no fact; it's to look at the actual evidence, a residual plot's shape, a description of how the sample was gathered, and use judgment about whether any departures are severe enough to be worth worrying about. A slightly bumpy residual plot from a sample of 50 is a very different situation from an obvious, strong curve in a sample of 50.

Running through all four conditions one more time for the hours-studied and quiz-score example ties the whole unit together. Linearity: the residuals (0, 0.2, −0.6, 0.6, −0.2, 0) show no curved pattern. Independence: reasonable, assuming the six students studied and were tested independently of one another. Normality: the small set of residuals looks roughly symmetric around 0, though six points is really too few to assess shape with much confidence. Equal variance: no obvious fanning across x = 1 through 6. With all four reasonably satisfied, the earlier t-test (t ≈ 16.84, df = 4, p < 0.0001) and t-interval ((1.50, 2.10)) can be treated as trustworthy summaries of this small illustrative dataset, keeping firmly in mind that a real study would want far more than six observations.

With conditions checked, the next step is writing an actual conclusion in context, and then, separately, asking whether a statistically real slope is also a big enough slope to matter.
